title: Milestone: How Hollywood Made Movies
objective: After this level you can connect the invention of film, the craft of shooting and cutting, and the studio system into one picture of how a classic Hollywood film was made.
summary: The studio era put every step of a film inside one company, from stars under contract and the Production Code to the studio's own theaters, until the 1948 Paramount ruling.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one classic Hollywood film to the screen.
cards.body: Fifty levels ago, a film was still frames flickering past a lamp. By the 1930s it was a product made on an assembly line, and one company could own every step. Here's the whole chain in one picture.

cards.headline: One film, one company, every step
cards.body: In the studio era, from about 1930 to 1945, a major studio carefully controlled every stage of a feature, from the first idea to the theater. Stars on seven-year contracts played the parts. The Production Code office had to approve the film. The studio's own distributors rented it out, often by the block, and its own first-run theaters showed it, at 24 frames a second, to paying crowds.

mascot.line: It connects: every level in this chapter is one link in that chain. Pull one link, and the rest move.

events.label: The Jazz Singer's success pushes Hollywood into sound

cards.headline: Milestone: the studio era, assembled
learned: How a studio made, sold and showed a film by itself, and why the 1948 ruling broke that chain.
Why sound, color and widescreen each changed how Hollywood shot and showed its films.
How the Production Code and the blacklist shaped what Hollywood said, and who could say it.
What makes Citizen Kane's deep focus, low angles and flashbacks worth studying.

questions.prompt: In the studio era, how much of a feature film's life did a major studio control?

options.label: Only the shooting; others handled the rest
options.rationale: The majors also distributed films and owned theaters.

options.label: Only the script, which it sold to theaters
options.rationale: The studio kept the film through every stage.

options.label: Every stage, from first idea to theater screen
None; the government ran production
options.rationale: Hollywood even wrote its own censorship code.

questions.explanation: From about 1930 to 1945, the studio system carefully controlled every stage of a feature, from conception through exhibition.

questions.prompt: Which studio's gamble on Vitaphone sound-on-disc led to The Jazz Singer?

options.label: MGM
options.rationale: MGM was a major, but the Vitaphone bet was Warner's.

options.label: Warner Brothers
RKO
options.rationale: RKO later released Citizen Kane.

options.label: Twentieth Century-Fox
options.rationale: Fox's big bet came later, with CinemaScope.

questions.explanation: Warner Brothers, then a minor studio, bought Vitaphone, debuted it in 1926 and followed with The Jazz Singer in 1927.

questions.prompt: How long did the standard studio-era star contract run?

options.label: One year
options.rationale: Much longer than that.

options.label: Three years
options.rationale: Still too short.

options.label: Seven years
Twenty years
options.rationale: De Havilland's fight was over a seven-year contract.

questions.explanation: The standard star contract ran seven years, which is why an extra six months mattered to Olivia de Havilland.

questions.prompt: Why did the 1952 Burstyn v. Wilson ruling weaken the Production Code?

options.label: It made block booking illegal
options.rationale: That was the 1948 Paramount case.

options.label: It gave the code office power to ban films
options.rationale: It worked the other way, loosening the code's grip.

options.label: It ordered studios to sell their theaters
options.rationale: That was the Paramount decrees of 1948.

options.label: It removed the threat of government censorship

questions.explanation: By ruling that films communicate ideas and can't face government censorship, the Court removed the threat the code was built to head off.

questions.prompt: Which link of Level 42's make-ship-show chain did the 1948 Paramount decrees cut away?

options.label: Showing: the studios' theater chains
Making: the studios' sound stages
options.rationale: The studios kept making films.

options.label: Starring: the seven-year contracts
options.rationale: Contracts were de Havilland's fight, not this case.

options.label: Approving: the Production Code office
options.rationale: The code lasted until 1968.

questions.explanation: The decrees forced the majors to sell their theater chains, separating production from exhibition.

questions.prompt: A film is a series of still photographs (Level 1). What did each frame of a three-strip Technicolor film start out as?

options.label: One photograph colored by hand after filming
options.rationale: The color came from dyes in printing, not paint.

options.label: A drawing traced from a filmed scene
options.rationale: It was photographed, not drawn.

options.label: A single color photograph on one strip
options.rationale: The camera held only black-and-white film.

options.label: Three black-and-white records of the same shot

questions.explanation: A beam-splitter sent the same image to three black-and-white strips, one each for red, green and blue.

questions.prompt: The Great Train Robbery (Level 8) cut between places happening at once. How does Citizen Kane move through its story instead?

options.label: In one unbroken shot from birth to death
options.rationale: It jumps back and forth in time.

options.label: Through flashbacks from people who knew Kane
Through intertitles read aloud by a narrator
options.rationale: It tells its story through witnesses' flashbacks.

options.label: By cutting between two cities at the same moment
options.rationale: That's closer to Level 8's cross-cutting.

questions.explanation: A reporter questions five people who knew Kane, and their shifting, not always reliable flashbacks build his life.
